patient.chief_complaint: Progressive right-sided headache, left arm weakness, and word-finding difficulty over 3 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 55-year-old right-handed South Asian male, a mathematics teacher, who presents with a 3-week history of progressive right-sided pulsatile headache, left arm weakness, and mild difficulty with calculations and word retrieval. He initially attributed the headache to stress and fatigue following a dental crown replacement procedure performed on his lower right first molar 3 weeks ago under local anesthesia. At that visit, the dentist noted mild peri-apical inflammation on pre-procedure radiograph, which was treated with the crown; the patient completed a 5-day prophylactic course of amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily post-procedure (completed approximately 2 weeks ago). His wife first noticed left arm clumsiness about 2 weeks ago when he kept dropping objects, and more recently he has had episodes of forgetting students' names and making arithmetic errors on the blackboard, which is completely out of character. He describes the headache as progressively worsening, worse in the morning and when bending forward, different in quality from any previous headaches, and not fully relieved by acetaminophen. He has had no seizures, no loss of consciousness, no fever at home (family noted 'he felt warm' on one occasion last week), no nausea or vomiting, no neck stiffness, and no rash. He denies weight loss, night sweats, or known exposure to sick contacts. On arrival to the emergency department, a non-contrast CT head was performed and revealed a ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal-parietal region with surrounding edema and mild mass effect, prompting urgent neurology admission and MRI. Given the recent dental procedure with documented peri-apical inflammation, the emergency physician charted an impression of 'ring-enhancing lesion — brain abscess vs. neoplasm, abscess more likely given dental source.'

results.title: Glioma grading: sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values of perfusion MR imaging and proton MR spectroscopy
results.authors: Law M, Yang S, Wang H, et al.
results.key_finding: Relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) >1.75 in the enhancing lesion has high sensitivity and specificity for high-grade glioma versus low-grade glioma. Brain abscesses demonstrate low rCBV (<1.0 in most series) because the enhancing rim reflects reactive inflammatory tissue without neovascularization, in contrast to the angiogenic vasculature of high-grade gliomas.

results.title: Potential of MR spectroscopy for assessment of glioma grading
results.authors: Bulik M, Jancalek R, Vanicek J, et al.
results.key_finding: Markedly elevated choline (Cho/NAA ratio >2.0, Cho/Cr ratio >2.5) with reduced NAA is characteristic of high-grade glioma. Pyogenic abscess shows absent or markedly reduced choline and NAA, with presence of amino acid peaks (succinate, acetate, alanine) at 1.3–1.9 ppm on short-echo MRS, which are absent in tumor.

results.title: The 2021 WHO classification of tumors of the central nervous system
results.authors: Louis DN, Perry A, Wesseling P, et al.
results.key_finding: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4 is defined by histological features (microvascular proliferation and/or necrosis) combined with IDH-wildtype status, and exhibits TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or +7/-10 chromosome pattern as molecular surrogates. Definitive diagnosis requires tissue. Imaging alone cannot distinguish GBM from abscess or metastasis with certainty.

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is not indicated in the diagnostic workup of a ring-enhancing brain mass. Regional slowing on EEG would be nonspecific and does not contribute to distinguishing tumor from abscess. No seizures are clinically documented in this case.
Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of a ring-enhancing brain mass in a patient without evidence of endocarditis or cardioembolic source.
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management in this case.

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated given the 5 mm midline shift, mass effect on the right lateral ventricle, and 3.4 cm mass lesion. LP creates a pressure gradient risking transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. CSF studies are also low-yield for the diagnosis of primary brain tumors.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture in a suspected mass lesion to identify mass effect and herniation risk; LP is contraindicated here given midline shift

critical_actions: Use DWI pattern (PERIPHERAL rim restriction vs. CENTRAL restriction) and MR perfusion rCBV to differentiate high-grade glioma from brain abscess before committing to a diagnosis

Order MR perfusion and MR spectroscopy as essential discriminators: high rCBV and elevated Cho without amino acid peaks favor neoplasm; low rCBV and amino acid peaks (acetate, succinate) favor abscess
Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for stereotactic biopsy with dual submission to neuropathology and microbiology — this simultaneously confirms histological diagnosis and excludes infection
Obtain MRI brain with gadolinium (tumor protocol with DWI) before any invasive procedure
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, CMP, coagulation, type and screen) and optimize glycemic control before craniotomy or biopsy
Initiate dexamethasone for symptomatic peritumoral edema; monitor blood glucose closely given T2DM — corticosteroids will worsen glycemic control and oral agents may be insufficient
Initiate levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis given mass effect and cortical involvement; preferred over enzyme-inducing AEDs due to no interaction with temozolomide
contraindicated_actions: Do not commit to treating as brain abscess and start empirical antibiotics without first reviewing DWI pattern (peripheral vs. central restriction), perfusion rCBV, and MRS amino acid peaks — premature antibiotic treatment delays tissue diagnosis of a fatal tumor
Do not perform lumbar puncture with 5 mm midline shift — herniation risk
Do not initiate tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not aspirate the lesion as a presumed abscess without intraoperative frozen-section confirmation — abscess aspiration without histology risks missing a neoplasm
key_reasoning_points: The critical DWI discriminator: pyogenic abscess causes CENTRAL restricted diffusion within the pus cavity (the central ADC is low); high-grade glioma causes PERIPHERAL restricted diffusion at the hypercellular enhancing rim (the central necrotic core has facilitated diffusion). This case shows peripheral rim restriction without central restriction — a pattern inconsistent with abscess.

MR perfusion (rCBV) is the most powerful non-invasive discriminator: abscess rCBV is low (<1.0) because the rim is reactive inflammatory tissue without tumor angiogenesis; high-grade glioma rCBV is markedly elevated (>1.75, often 2.5-4.0) due to pathological neovascularization. rCBV 3.1 in this case excludes abscess.

MR spectroscopy provides additional discrimination: abscess produces amino acid peaks (acetate at 1.92 ppm, succinate at 2.4 ppm, alanine at 1.47 ppm) from bacterial fermentation; high-grade glioma produces elevated Cho/NAA without these peaks. Absence of amino acid peaks in this case further argues against abscess.

The low-grade fever (37.9°C), mildly elevated CRP/ESR, and recent dental procedure are classic red herrings that anchor toward abscess; however, procalcitonin is normal, blood cultures are negative, and the dental source was minor (crown replacement, not abscess drainage with uncontrolled infection) — the infective source is insufficient to explain a 3.4 cm intracranial lesion.

Irregular nodular rim enhancement is a morphological feature favoring neoplasm; abscess typically produces a thin, smooth, medially thin-walled ring (the medial wall is thinner due to differential blood supply). This case shows a thick, irregular, nodular rim — inconsistent with the expected abscess morphology.
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue — stereotactic biopsy with dual submission to pathology and microbiology ensures that abscess is microbiologically excluded even if imaging strongly favors tumor.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests an active infectious process, anchoring toward brain abscess as the unifying diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Low-grade fever is non-specific and may accompany peritumoral inflammation or steroid-mediated cytokine release in high-grade glioma; procalcitonin is normal and blood cultures are negative — does not support bacteremia or systemic bacterial infection

red_herrings.data_point: Recent dental crown replacement with documented peri-apical inflammation 3 weeks ago, followed by a 5-day prophylactic amoxicillin course
red_herrings.intended_effect: Provides a plausible odontogenic source for hematogenous brain abscess, anchoring the emergency physician (and potentially the agent) toward abscess as the leading diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A dental crown procedure with prophylactic antibiotic coverage is a low-risk source for intracranial abscess; the DWI pattern (peripheral, not central restriction), high rCBV (3.1), elevated Cho without amino acid peaks, and negative blood cultures and procalcitonin all argue decisively against abscess; the temporal coincidence is misleading

red_herrings.data_point: Mildly elevated CRP (2.2 mg/dL) and ESR (31 mm/hr) with normal WBC and procalcitonin
red_herrings.intended_effect: Mild inflammatory marker elevation consistent with systemic infection, reinforcing the abscess anchoring impression
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CRP and ESR elevations are non-specific; tumors, particularly high-grade gliomas, can drive systemic inflammatory responses. Normal procalcitonin is a strong negative predictor for bacterial infection; normal WBC without left shift does not support active bacterial sepsis

metadata.diagnostic_challenge_notes: This is the first GBM-vs-abscess ring-enhancement diagnostic puzzle in the GLIO-HG set. The case tests whether the agent correctly interprets the DWI pattern (peripheral vs. central restriction), orders and integrates MR perfusion (high rCBV excludes abscess) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho without amino acid peaks excludes abscess), and resists premature closure on the abscess diagnosis despite three embedded red herrings (low-grade fever, recent dental procedure with peri-apical inflammation, and mildly elevated CRP/ESR). The emergency physician's impression of 'abscess more likely' is a deliberate anchoring cue that a competent agent must override via systematic imaging interpretation.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools (MRI, labs, literature search, neurosurgery consult, neuro-oncology consult), 2 recommended tools (perfusion MRI, MR spectroscopy), 3 embedded red herrings (fever, dental history, inflammatory markers); requires cross-modal synthesis of DWI pattern + rCBV + MRS amino acid absence to exclude abscess; ER physician anchoring cue adds cognitive anchoring pressure
